questions.question: What does SSH stand for?

explanation.correct: SSH stands for Secure Shell — a protocol for encrypted remote login.
explanation.why: A is made up; C and D are incorrect expansions.

questions.question: By default, Amazon Linux supports which login method?

explanation.correct: Amazon Linux uses SSH key-based authentication by default for security.
explanation.why: Password-based auth is disabled by default. OTP and certificate methods require extra setup.

questions.question: Where is the SSH private key stored?

explanation.correct: The private key is always stored on your local machine. The public key goes on the server.
explanation.why: Storing the private key on the server defeats its purpose. IAM and S3 are AWS services unrelated to SSH key storage.

questions.question: In which file on the server is the SSH public key stored?

explanation.correct: The public key is placed in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server.
explanation.why: id_rsa.pub is the public key file on your laptop. known_hosts stores verified server fingerprints. sshd_config is the SSH daemon configuration.

questions.question: What is the permission type that allows a user to run a script file?

explanation.correct: Execute (x) permission allows a user to run a file as a program or script.
explanation.why: Read allows viewing, write allows editing, and 'modify' is just another name for write — not a separate Linux permission type.

questions.question: Which command shows file permissions, owner, and group in Linux?

explanation.correct: ls -l (long listing) shows permissions, number of links, owner, group, size, date, and filename.
explanation.why: ls -a shows hidden files; ls -r reverses sort order; ls -p appends / to directories but doesn't show permission details.

questions.question: In a permission string '-rw-r--r--', what permissions does the group have?

explanation.correct: Characters 5-7 represent group permissions. 'r--' means read only — write and execute are denied.
explanation.why: The full string: - (file type), rw- (owner: read+write), r-- (group: read only), r-- (others: read only).

questions.question: What does the first character 'd' in a permission string indicate?

options.text: The file is a symbolic link
The file belongs to the root user

explanation.correct: The first character in the permission string indicates the file type. 'd' means it is a directory.
explanation.why: '-' means regular file; 'l' means symbolic link; file type has nothing to do with delete permissions or ownership.

questions.question: What does chmod 755 set for group permissions?

explanation.correct: In 755: 7=owner(rwx), 5=group(r-x), 5=others(r-x). Value 5 = 4(read)+1(execute).

questions.question: Which command changes the owner of a file?

explanation.correct: chown (change owner) is the command to change file ownership.
explanation.why: chmod changes permissions; chgrp changes only the group; chperm does not exist.

questions.question: What does the umask value 022 result in for newly created files?

explanation.correct: Files max at 666; 666 - 022 = 644 (rw-r--r--). Directories would get 755.
explanation.why: Files don't get execute by default (max 666 not 777). Subtracting 022 from 666 gives 644.

questions.question: How many bits does the -b 4096 option set when generating an SSH key?

explanation.correct: -b 4096 explicitly sets the key length to 4096 bits, which is stronger than the default 2048.
explanation.why: The -b flag directly sets the bit count. 4096 is the value given in the command.

questions.question: A file has permissions 'drwx------'. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Only the owner can read, write, and enter the directory
The group can read the directory

explanation.correct: drwx------ means: d=directory, rwx=owner full access, ---=group nothing, ---=others nothing.
explanation.why: The last 6 dashes mean group and others have zero permissions. Only the owner (u=rwx) has access.

questions.question: Which command would you use to check the permissions of a directory itself (not its contents)?

explanation.correct: ls -ld shows the permissions of the directory object itself. Without -d, ls -l lists the directory's contents.
explanation.why: ls -l lists what's inside; -a shows hidden files; -r reverses order. The -d flag is specifically for listing directory metadata.

questions.question: What does the -C flag do in the ssh-keygen command?

options.text: Adds a comment/label to the key

explanation.correct: -C adds a comment (label) to the SSH key — typically your email address — to help identify the key.
explanation.why: -t sets the type/algorithm; -b sets bit strength; -C (capital) is specifically the comment flag.

questions.question: To enable password-based SSH login on Amazon Linux, which file must be edited?

explanation.correct: The SSH daemon config at /etc/ssh/sshd_config controls server-side SSH settings including PasswordAuthentication.
explanation.why: authorized_keys stores public keys; ssh_config is the client config; /etc/passwd stores user account info but not SSH settings.

questions.question: What permission must execute on a directory allow you to do?

explanation.correct: Execute on a directory means you can cd into it — without execute, you cannot traverse into the directory.
explanation.why: Listing requires read; deleting and creating require write. Execute on a directory specifically controls traversal/entry.

questions.question: Which command copies your SSH public key to a remote server?

explanation.correct: ssh-copy-id automatically appends your public key to the remote user's authorized_keys file.
explanation.why: scp and rsync can transfer files but don't handle the authorized_keys format automatically. ssh-keygen --copy does not exist.

questions.question: A developer needs other users to be able to read a file but not modify it. What chmod command achieves this?

explanation.correct: chmod o+r adds read permission to others without adding write or execute.
explanation.why: o+rw adds both read and write. o=rwx sets all permissions for others. a+r adds read to everyone — which may not be desired if only others need it.

questions.question: On Windows, SSH connection fails because two files are named 'key.pem' and 'Key.pem'. Why is this a problem?

options.text: Windows is case-insensitive and treats them as the same file, causing conflicts
Linux key files cannot be used on Windows
The file extension .pem is not supported on Windows

explanation.correct: Windows is case-insensitive. Two files named 'key.pem' and 'Key.pem' are treated as duplicates, causing SSH to be unable to read the key correctly.
explanation.why: Windows does support .pem files. The issue is specifically Windows case-insensitivity causing file conflicts. Linux keys work fine on Windows with the right tools.

questions.question: What is the numeric chmod value for a file that should be readable and writable by the owner, readable by the group, and inaccessible to others?

explanation.correct: 640: owner=rw(6), group=r(4), others=none(0). This gives the group read access while blocking others entirely.
explanation.why: 644 also gives others read access; 600 blocks the group too; 660 gives group write access which wasn't required.

questions.question: What does the SUID (Set User ID) permission do when set on an executable?

options.text: The file runs with the permissions of the user who launched it
The file runs with the permissions of the file's owner
The file can only be run by the root user
The file's execute bit is removed after first run

explanation.correct: SUID makes the executable run with the file owner's permissions, not the launching user's. The passwd command uses this to allow regular users to modify /etc/shadow.
explanation.why: Without SUID, the file runs with the launching user's permissions. SUID doesn't restrict to root or auto-remove permissions.

questions.question: The sticky bit is set on /tmp. What does this mean for users?

options.text: Only the file's owner, directory owner, or root can delete files inside /tmp
No new files can be created in /tmp

explanation.correct: The sticky bit prevents users from deleting other users' files even if they have write access to the directory.
explanation.why: Files are not read-only — users can still create and write their own files. The sticky bit only affects deletion by non-owners.

questions.question: A security team requires that SSH private key files on EC2 instances have chmod 400. What is the reasoning?

options.text: chmod 400 is the only value that allows SSH to read the file
SSH refuses to use key files that are accessible to group or others, and 400 restricts access to owner-read only
chmod 400 encrypts the private key at rest
AWS mandates chmod 400 for compliance reasons

explanation.correct: The SSH client enforces that private key files are not too open. If group or others can read the key, SSH will throw 'WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!' and refuse to connect. chmod 400 (owner read-only) satisfies this requirement.
explanation.why: chmod 400 does not encrypt the file. AWS recommends it but SSH's own security check is the primary enforcement mechanism.

questions.question: Which octal value correctly represents chmod permissions for a script that the owner can fully access, group members can read and execute, but others cannot access at all?

explanation.correct: 750: owner=rwx(7), group=r-x(5), others=---(0). Group gets read+execute but no write. Others are completely blocked.
explanation.why: 755 would give others r-x access. 740 would give group only read (no execute). 770 would give group write access.

questions.question: An admin runs 'chmod -R 777 /' accidentally on a production server. What is the most critical security risk?

options.text: All files and directories get full permissions for everyone, allowing any user to modify system files

explanation.correct: chmod -R 777 / gives every user (including malicious ones) read, write, and execute on everything — including /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and system binaries. This is a catastrophic security failure.
explanation.why: Files remain readable, the server stays up, and root access is not affected — but the system becomes completely insecure.

questions.question: A user creates a file inside a directory with SGID set. What group does the new file inherit?

explanation.correct: SGID on a directory causes newly created files to inherit the directory's group, not the creating user's primary group. This is essential for shared team directories.
explanation.why: Without SGID, files would inherit the creator's primary group. Root group and no-group scenarios don't apply here.

questions.question: How do you change only the group of a file to 'devteam' without changing the owner?

explanation.correct: chown :devteam (with colon and no username before it) changes only the group. The empty username before the colon leaves the owner unchanged.
explanation.why: chown devteam (without colon) changes the owner, not the group. chmod changes permissions, not ownership. chperm doesn't exist.

questions.question: In a team scenario, a DevOps engineer must ensure that files created in /shared/project are always owned by the 'devops' group so all team members can access them. What is the best approach?

options.text: Run chown -R :devops /shared/project after every file creation
Set sticky bit on the /shared/project directory

explanation.correct: SGID on a directory ensures all new files created inside automatically inherit the directory's group ('devops'). This is the standard solution for shared team directories.
explanation.why: Manual chown after every creation is error-prone. SUID on directories has different behavior. Sticky bit prevents deletion by non-owners but doesn't affect group inheritance.

questions.question: What happens when you run 'ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C email@example.com' and the ~/.ssh/id_rsa file already exists?

options.text: The command fails with a fatal error
The existing key is automatically backed up
You are prompted to confirm before overwriting the existing key
A new key is created with a timestamp suffix

explanation.correct: ssh-keygen detects the existing file and asks 'Overwrite (y/n)?' before proceeding. This prevents accidental loss of an existing key pair.
explanation.why: The command does not fail, auto-backup, or create timestamped variants. The overwrite prompt is a safety feature built into ssh-keygen.
